record.paper_title: (Two) Open Questions in Stellar Nuclear Physics
record.context_brief: C/O ratio and 12C(α,γ)16O extrapolation for stellar evolution and SNeIa
record.original_question: How can the carbon-to-oxygen ratio at the end of helium burning be determined accurately enough for massive-star evolution and Type Ia supernova light-curve modeling, given that the 12C(α,γ)16O cross section is needed near 300 keV but has only been measured down to about 1.2 MeV, R-matrix extrapolation uncertainties cannot be substantiated, and published E1 and E2 astrophysical S-factor determinations disagree substantially?

evidence.quote: The C/O ratio at the end of helium burning is still poorly known, twenty years after it was declared by Willie Fowler the "holy grail" of Nuclear Astro-Physics [14]. This parameter is essential for almost all aspects of stellar evolution of massive stars, and most recently it was also suggested to be essential for understanding the light curve of SNeIa [15].

In order to measure the C/O ratio at the end of helium burning the cross section of the 12C(α,γ)16O needs to be known at approximately 300 keV , but thus far it wasmeasured only down to approximately 1.2 MeV . The extrapolation of this cross section to stellar energies (300 keV) is particularly difficult due to the substantial contribution from bound states.

However, it now appears that the claimed accuracy of the R-matrix fits can not be substantiated. While the TRIUMF group quote an E1 astrophysical cross section factor with 25 % uncertainty [17], Hale extracts a value that is eight times smaller [18]. Similarlyelastic scattering data was used by the Notre Dame group to extract the E2 S-factor with the claimed 20% accuracy [19]. But this analysis in of itself was criticized for lack of theoretical foundation [20], and the result turned out to be a factor of 2.5 smaller than extracted by the Stuttgart group [21]

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the radiative-capture reaction $^{12}\mathrm{C}(\alpha,\gamma)^{16}\mathrm{O}$, whose rate at the stellar helium-burning Gamow energy $E_{\mathrm{c.m.}} \approx 300$ keV controls the carbon-to-oxygen (C/O) ratio produced at the end of core helium burning. Write the cross section as
$$\sigma(E) = \frac{S(E)}{E}\,\exp\!\left(-2\pi\eta(E)\right),$$
where $\eta(E)$ is the Sommerfeld parameter and $S(E)$ is the astrophysical $S$-factor, decomposed into multipole contributions $S_{E1}(E)$ and $S_{E2}(E)$ from the electric-dipole and electric-quadrupole transitions to the $^{16}\mathrm{O}$ ground state (which depend on subthreshold $1^-$ and $2^+$ bound-state contributions as well as broad resonances).

Direct laboratory measurements of $\sigma(E)$ are limited to $E_{\mathrm{c.m.}} \gtrsim 1.2$ MeV, so the values $S_{E1}(300\text{ keV})$ and $S_{E2}(300\text{ keV})$ must be obtained by extrapolation (typically via multilevel $R$-matrix analyses) constrained by capture, elastic-scattering, $\beta$-delayed $\alpha$-spectrum, and photodisintegration data. Published extrapolations disagree by factors of several, and the C/O ratio at the end of helium burning, required for modeling massive-star evolution and Type Ia supernova light curves, depends sensitively on these values.

Problem: Determine $S_{E1}(300\text{ keV})$ and $S_{E2}(300\text{ keV})$ (and hence the total $S$-factor and reaction rate of $^{12}\mathrm{C}(\alpha,\gamma)^{16}\mathrm{O}$ at 300 keV) with a total uncertainty small enough (target: better than $\sim 10\%$) to fix the post-helium-burning C/O ratio to the precision required by stellar-evolution and Type Ia supernova light-curve modeling, with rigorously substantiated error bars.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature, including a 2025 European Physical Journal A review and ongoing experimental programs (HIγS photodisintegration, ERNA, LUNA-MV, JUNA), shows that the $^{12}\mathrm{C}(\alpha,\gamma)^{16}\mathrm{O}$ $S$-factor at 300 keV remains undetermined to the precision required. Different $R$-matrix analyses still give $S(300)$ values spanning roughly 140–170 keV·b with quoted uncertainties of $\sim 15$–25%, and $E1$/$E2$ decompositions continue to disagree. The reaction is still described as a central open problem in nuclear astrophysics.

status_evidence.title: The 12C(α,γ)16O reaction, in the laboratory and in the stars
status_evidence.snippet: Review (2025) describing continued discrepancies and uncertainties in S(300) for 12C(α,γ)16O.
status_evidence.claim: The reaction's S-factor at stellar energies remains uncertain and is still considered a key open problem.

status_evidence.title: The astrophysical S factor of 12C(α,γ)16O at stellar energy
status_evidence.snippet: Reports S(300) ≈ 161 ± 19 keV b with ~12% uncertainty from a global R-matrix fit.
status_evidence.claim: Best fits still carry ~12–15% uncertainties and depend on extrapolation models.

status_evidence.title: 16O(e,e'α)12C measurements and the 12C(α,γ)16O astrophysical reaction rate
status_evidence.snippet: Recent indirect measurement aimed at constraining the subthreshold contributions to S(300).
status_evidence.claim: New indirect-measurement efforts are ongoing to reduce extrapolation uncertainty.
